why: The statement is a universal conjecture (τ ≤ (r−1)ν for every r and every r-partite H), so a counterexample at even one rank answers it in the negative. The OpenAI manuscripts claim intersecting counterexamples at infinitely many ranks, with no earlier refutation on record, so they are scored whole/refuted/counterexample. They are unreviewed: Lean modules read sorry-free but were not rebuilt, and F7 applies in any case. No specific error was identified, so they are credible. The AI role is generated: the release has no human author and attributes its results to the internal model. White's (4,2) and Kitamura's (4,3) results are restrictions to single (r,ν) pairs, so they are case. White's Methods credit the model with finding the key lemma and the proof itself, with the human checking it computationally, so that is generated. Kitamura's disclosure says only 'with assistance' and assigns no part to any tool, so per F12 it is none. The Lovász-deletion, coloured-graph, bounded-diameter and Latin-square papers address different statements: variant. Tuza's unproved (4,2) claim settles nothing, and Haxell–Scott 2016 is a sharpness construction that the statement does not ask about; both are none.
doubts: openai-math-162 bundles the same two manuscripts recorded separately as openai-2026-p-power-plus-one-counterexample (23 Sep) and openai-2026-balanced-prime-q (27 Sep); its 6 Oct date is the release date, not the first written argument. All three are the same work. The AI attribution for the OpenAI events rests on a release-level README sentence; no per-paper statement was read. Kitamura's ν=3 result reportedly depends on White's unreviewed Lemma 2.2. The statement does not spell out r-partiteness; the standard reading was used.
